consensus_summary: All three blind responses converge on the same core: the 'new name' symbolizes a new God-given identity, character, and status conferred on the redeemed/overcomer — a transformation of the person and their standing before God, with eschatological acceptance. Alternatives include a secret name of personal intimacy, Christ's/God's name marking ownership, corporate covenantal restoration of Zion, and background readings (admission token, literal name).
book_summary: The book identifies the 'new name' as the renewed covenant itself, which is known — and, in the book's wordplay, kept — only by the one who receives it. It explicitly flags the common teaching (a new God-given identity and character bestowed on the overcomer) as the view it departs from.
consensus_core_identification: New name = a divinely bestowed new identity/character/status for the redeemed person (or restored people), marking transformation and eschatological acceptance.
book_core_identification: New name = the renewed covenant between God and the recipient, individually known and kept by that recipient alone.
boundary_disagreement: The book reinterprets the same proof texts (Jacob/Israel, Isaiah 62, Revelation 2:17) so that the name signifies not the person's transformed identity but the covenant relationship itself; it also reads 'knoweth' in Rev 2:17 as covenant-keeping ('known — kept'), a condition absent from the consensus readings.
material_contradiction: The consensus says the name IS the believer's new identity/character; the book says the name IS the renewed covenant. The book's own common-view note marks the identity/character reading as the teaching it replaces, so accepting the book's identification requires rejecting the consensus's central referent, not merely adjusting its boundary. A covenant received and kept is a relational bond, not a bestowed personal identity.
rationale: Both readings use the same passages, but the central referent differs: identity/character bestowed on the person versus the covenant itself received and kept by the person. The closest consensus alternatives (corporate covenantal restoration in Isaiah; personal intimacy in Rev 2:17) treat covenant as context or effect, not as the identification of the name itself. Because the book explicitly contrasts itself with the commonly taught identity reading and substitutes 'renewed covenant' as what the name is, this is replacement of the central referent (DIVERGENT), not a narrowing or refinement of the identity reading. It is not NOVEL-without-contradiction because the book itself frames its reading against the consensus view.
strongest_objection: One could argue the readings are compatible rather than contradictory — a covenant renaming (Abraham, Israel, Hephzibah/Beulah) simultaneously confers a new identity, and Isaiah 62's marriage imagery is covenantal, so 'renewed covenant' might be a NOVEL emphasis or a COMPATIBLE_OVERLAP refinement rather than a replacement. The classification as DIVERGENT rests on the book's explicit common-view note signaling departure and on its substitution of what the name fundamentally is.
